Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

Clinical Vignette: Priya

Priya was sixty-one years old when she came to the clinic, though the weight she carried made her seem older. She had worked the fields outside Fresno for nearly forty years-harvesting almonds and cotton, her hands callused and her back permanently curved from decades of bending. She was married to Rajesh, a quiet man who worked construction, and they had two adult children who lived in the city. To anyone who knew her only from the farm, Priya was reliable, efficient, and unobtrusive. What almost no one knew was that she had been raped in the irrigation ditch behind the fields in 1998, by a man whose face she could still see with perfect clarity when she closed her eyes at night.

The attack had happened on a late afternoon in September, when she had gone to the far corner of the property to check the water flow. A man had emerged from behind the equipment shed-someone she did not know, someone who had no business being there. He had forced her down into the ditch, and what followed was an assault that lasted, she believed, though she could never be certain, perhaps fifteen minutes. She had screamed, but the nearest workers were too far away, and the sound of the irrigation pump had drowned her out. When it was over, he had run toward the road, and she had lain there in the dirt and water, her clothes torn, her body shaking so violently she could not stand.

For the first few years after the assault, Priya had told almost no one. She had cleaned herself, changed her clothes, and returned to work the next day. She had not reported it to the police-a choice born partly from shame, partly from a fear of the police themselves, partly from the belief that nothing would come of it anyway. She had tried to continue as though the afternoon had been erased. But the mind, she had come to understand, does not permit such erasure. By 2000, the symptoms had begun to crystallize into the pattern that now defined her life.

The triggers were specific and inescapable. Dogs, first and foremost: she had heard the dog barking just before the man had appeared that day, a sound that had seemed, in retrospect, like a warning she had not heeded. Now, whenever she heard barking-at a neighbor's fence, or in the distance as she walked to the market-her entire body seized with dread. The memory would come without warning, fully formed and overwhelming, as though the ditch and the man and the violation were happening again in real time, her heart hammering against her ribs as though she were still pinned beneath him. Sexual situations triggered the same response: when Rajesh would reach for her in the night, her body would react before her mind could catch up. She would flinch, or her breathing would become shallow, or a wave of nausea would rise in her throat. She had come to dread intimacy with a terror that seemed to bypass thought altogether-her nervous system had learned to interpret her husband's touch as a threat, and no amount of reasoning could convince her body otherwise.

The memories themselves had become a kind of torment. They would arrive unbidden, often triggered by something as mundane as the smell of irrigation water or the sight of a man in a dark shirt. When they came, they did not arrive as a narrative she could observe from a distance; instead, they replayed like a film she was forced to watch from inside the screen, her body present in the ditch, the panic as immediate and real as it had been twenty-five years ago. She would lie awake at night, her mind cycling through the memory, unable to sleep because some part of her remained convinced that she needed to stay alert, to watch for danger, to ensure that nothing like this could happen again. When Rajesh would move suddenly in bed, or when the neighbor's dog would bark at three in the morning, she would startle violently, her body bracing for attack. The hypervigilance had become so habitual that she could no longer distinguish between genuine threat and the phantom danger her nervous system had been trained to expect.

Over the years, this vigilance had begun to erode her life. She had stopped going to the far fields, which meant her income had decreased and her work had become more limited. She had begun to avoid being alone, yet she also could not bear to be touched. She had become withdrawn from Rajesh, who loved her but could not understand why his wife flinched from his hand. She came to the clinic because her daughter had insisted, because she was exhausted in a way that sleep could no longer touch, and because she was afraid-not just of the memory, but of the possibility that she might live the rest of her life imprisoned by it.
